summary: Psalm 128 blesses the person who fears Yahweh and walks in his ways. It moves from the individual's work and household to a wider prayer for Zion, Jerusalem, future generations, and Israel's peace.
whyItMatters: This short Song of Ascents connects reverent daily life with household flourishing and the welfare of Jerusalem. Inside Book V of Psalms, it fits the collection's emphasis on pilgrimage, worship, and communal hope.

context.author: Psalms is an anthology with many writers and collections; this psalm's heading identifies it as a Song of Ascents but does not name an author.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping community, especially readers or singers who understood pilgrimage and Zion as central images of worship.
context.date: The Psalms were composed and collected over time; the exact date of Psalm 128 is uncertain.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, among the Songs of Ascents, poems associated with movement toward worship and Jerusalem.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and blessing, moving from wisdom-like description to prayer.

outline.heading: The blessed way
outline.note: The psalm opens by blessing everyone who fears Yahweh and walks in his ways.

outline.heading: Work that sustains
outline.note: The blessing is pictured as eating the labor of one's hands and living with well-being.

outline.heading: Household fruitfulness
outline.note: The home is described through images of a fruitful vine and olive shoots, then summed up as the blessing of the one who fears Yahweh.

outline.heading: Blessing from Zion
outline.note: The prayer widens from one household to Yahweh's blessing out of Zion and the good of Jerusalem.

outline.heading: Generations and peace
outline.note: The final wish reaches to children's children and ends with peace upon Israel.

keyVerses.text: A Song of Ascents. Blessed is everyone who fears Yahweh, who walks in his ways.
keyVerses.why: This line gives the psalm's heading and its central claim: blessing belongs to those who revere Yahweh and live in his ways.

keyVerses.text: For you will eat the labor of your hands. You will be happy, and it will be well with you.
keyVerses.why: This verse makes the blessing concrete in ordinary work, food, happiness, and well-being.

keyVerses.text: May Yahweh bless you out of Zion, and may you see the good of Jerusalem all the days of your life.
keyVerses.why: Here the psalm turns from description to prayer and connects the household's good with Zion and Jerusalem.

keyVerses.text: Yes, may you see your children’s children. Peace be upon Israel.
keyVerses.why: The closing line stretches the blessing across generations and ends with a prayer for Israel's peace.

themes: Fear of Yahweh and walking in his ways

questions.question: What is a Song of Ascents?
questions.answer: The heading places this psalm among the Songs of Ascents. The group belongs to Book V’s pilgrimage material, but the heading does not identify one exact performance setting for this psalm.

questions.question: What does it mean here to fear Yahweh?
questions.answer: In this chapter, fearing Yahweh is paired with walking in his ways. The psalm presents it as reverent loyalty shown in a person's way of life, not as panic or mere private emotion.

questions.question: Who is called blessed in this psalm?
questions.answer: The opening says, "everyone who fears Yahweh, who walks in his ways." Verse 4 repeats the idea in singular form: "the man who fears Yahweh." The movement from "everyone" to "the man" gives the blessing both a broad and a household-focused shape.

questions.question: Does verse 2 promise that faithful people will always prosper?
questions.answer: Psalm 128 depicts blessing through work, food, happiness, and well-being. Readers differ on how to relate such wisdom-like blessing language to the many psalms where faithful speakers suffer or wait without relief. This chapter states the blessing positively; it does not discuss exceptions or explain every case of hardship.

questions.question: Why compare the wife to a fruitful vine and children to olive shoots?
questions.answer: The images in verse 3 picture vitality and fruitfulness inside the household. The verse uses agricultural images to describe family life around the house and table. It is poetic imagery, not a full statement about every person's family situation.

questions.question: Why does the psalm move from one family to Jerusalem?
questions.answer: The psalm begins with the blessed person and household, then prays, "May Yahweh bless you out of Zion." The good of the household is set within the good of Jerusalem, so personal blessing and communal worship are not isolated from each other.

questions.question: What is Zion in this verse?
questions.answer: The chapter names Zion as the place from which Yahweh's blessing is asked. Zion names Jerusalem as the center of worship; this verse links blessing from Zion with seeing the good of Jerusalem.

questions.question: Why does seeing children's children matter here?
questions.answer: Verse 6 extends the blessing beyond immediate well-being to another generation. In the flow of the psalm, the household image of verse 3 becomes a wish for long life and continuity.

questions.question: Why end with peace upon Israel?
questions.answer: The last sentence widens the prayer one final time. The psalm has moved from everyone who fears Yahweh, to one household, to Jerusalem, and finally to Israel. The ending keeps private blessing inside the life of the whole people.

glossary.def: The divine name used in this translation. In this psalm, Yahweh is the one to be feared and the one asked to bless from Zion.
Named in verse 5 as the source from which Yahweh's blessing is requested, paired with the good of Jerusalem.
The city whose good the speaker prays the blessed person will see all the days of life.
An image for children around the table, suggesting young growth and household fruitfulness.
